articles.title: Football Daily | West Ham want promotion – so it’s time to call in an understated club legend
articles.summary: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! While Football Daily hasn’t actually seen much of West Ham this season, we’ve noted enough of their results to presume they were doing OK in their attempt to bounce back to the Premier League after…
articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! While Football Daily hasn’t actually seen much of West Ham this season, we’ve noted enough of their results to presume they were doing OK in their attempt to bounce back to the Premier League after relegation. Less than a third of the way through the Championship season under Nuno Espírito Santo, they’d already spanked six without reply past both Wrexham and Lincoln, while scoring three or more in wins over Wolves, Derby and Bolton. However, it turns out that of the 13 matches they’ve played in a league that is famously difficult to get out of (unless you were Sheffield Wednesday last season ), they have actually lost three times and currently sit in eighth place, a whopping six points off leaders Middlesbrough. Given the context of such an unbridgeable chasm, it is small wonder West Ham fans woke up to news that Nuno had been unceremoniously bounced out of the London Stadium with a P45 in hand. While my heart aches for Jesús de Miguel, who has died after a collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono, I shudder to think the trauma that shall haunt Owono for the rest of his life. I do hope and pray the wider community understands and extends their support in his recuperation” – Krishna Moorthy. As an upgrade to Steve Plever’s suggestion of paper thin shirts [ Monday’s letters ]: how about Velcro shirts? If the bit comes off, it is a shirt pull and the offender has the honour of putting it back in place before being awarded a yellow card” – Mike Harold. To dive or not to dive seems to be biggest dilemma in the Premier League right now. It’s not. The problem with today’s highly paid professionals is that they simply have no panache at all when they go down. I recall watching Francis Lee pick up the ball on the halfway line at a mud soaked Maine Road in the late 1960s, he put his head down and headed for goal, he was determined, he was single minded. He was 30 yards from goal, he was in full flow. He was tackled from behind and then he really took off, he grew wings, he soared. I swear he landed in the penalty area over 10 yards away. He dragged himself to his feet and without a semblance of a smile smashed the well-deserved penalty, with a very heavy leather ball straight at the centre of the goal at over 70 mph. The goalkeeper, obviously no fool, simply dived out of the way. The press christened him “Lee Won Pen” He was my hero. That man had panache, he had style” – Myles Flynn. I am interested to read that Aston Villa considered the words of Jamie Carragher “unacceptable insults” . It would obviously help matters if they could publish examples of acceptable insults” – Rupert Jeffery. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. articles.title: Juan Atkins built a cybernetic future for music – but invested it with humanity
articles.summary: The Detroit techno pioneer, who has died aged 64 , blended funk and electronics with information-age philosophy to create music of huge power and influence Juan Atkins, the originator of techno who died on 31 October, spent his lifetime translating a…
articles.content: The Detroit techno pioneer, who has died aged 64 , blended funk and electronics with information-age philosophy to create music of huge power and influence Juan Atkins, the originator of techno who died on 31 October, spent his lifetime translating a fascination with the future into sound. He was the oldest of the founding fathers of techno known as the “Belleville Three”, along with his junior high school friends Kevin Saunderson and Derrick May. He was the first of the trio to buy a Korg MS-10 synthesiser, and also taught the others how to DJ on turntables. His work in the duo Cybotron alongside Rik Davis was the sonic blueprint that sketched out what later became known as techno – indeed, he is the one who gave the genre its name. Without Atkins, and the way he empowered those around him, electronic music certainly would not exist in its current form today. Continue reading...

articles.title: Carrie at 50: Brian De Palma’s fiery masterpiece still has the power
articles.summary: The Oscar-nominated 1976 adaptation of Stephen King’s high school horror remains heartbreaking and horrifying in equal measure Often when a pop culture figure, whether real or fictional or somewhere in between, is described as an eternal teenager, it refers…
articles.content: The Oscar-nominated 1976 adaptation of Stephen King’s high school horror remains heartbreaking and horrifying in equal measure Often when a pop culture figure, whether real or fictional or somewhere in between, is described as an eternal teenager, it refers to an image of youthful vitality. Carrie White, the wallflowery, telekinetic, sort-of heroine at the center of Stephen King’s book and its multiple adaptations, is a sadder case. She’s forever a teenager because until recently, every version of the story ends with her demise – a turn that would qualify as a spoiler if not for the universal familiarity of her story, or the fact that the book heavily implies her fate within the first 30 pages or so. That fate is poised to change with Mike Flanagan’s TV series , which was recently renewed for a second season (though even then, there’s still plenty of room for poor Carrie to die young). The new show updates and expands the story of the 1974 novel, taking its inspiration from a combination of 2020s social trends and details from the original text. In other words, it’s a new adaptation, not a remake of the Brian De Palma film from 1976. As such, it’s the first truly successful version of Carrie in half a century. (Previous iterations popped up in a 1999 movie sequel, a 2002 miniseries and another film in 2013 .) It’s arguable, however, that the reason such a high-profile new version of Carrie exists in 2026 is that first film, which was released 50 years ago on 3 November. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK also affected by supermarket fridge hacks, cyber chief says
articles.summary: Supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden and Belgium reported fridges being hiked in temperature on Monday.
articles.content: Supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden and Belgium reported fridges being hiked in temperature on Monday.
articles.aiArticle:
Retail stores across the United Kingdom have faced the same malicious cyber intrusion that recently compromised grocery refrigeration units in several other European nations, according to British cybersecurity authorities. 

British supermarkets are currently dealing with security breaches that secretly tamper with industrial cooling equipment, leaving perishable goods vulnerable to spoilage. 

## International Reach and Security Warnings

The sophisticated digital disruption first came to light on **Monday**, when retail outlets across **Ireland**, **Sweden**, and **Belgium** discovered unauthorized actors maliciously raising the temperatures inside their commercial refrigerators. While the initial wave of attacks primarily targeted continental Europe, British officials confirmed the threat has now crossed the Channel to affect domestic locations. 

According to BBC News, the UK's cyber chief verified that British establishments are among those impacted by these strange temperature hacks. Security teams across multiple chains are scrambling to lock down connected refrigeration infrastructure and prevent further spoilage incidents.

## Understanding the Retail Threat

Food safety protocols rely heavily on strict temperature controls to keep perishable inventory safe for consumers. When unauthorized individuals gain remote access to refrigeration units, the commercial implications can quickly escalate from logistical headaches to massive financial losses and public health concerns. Understanding [who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/who-is-hacking-europe-s-supermarket-fridges-and-freezers-and-why) remains a primary objective for investigators attempting to trace the digital signatures left behind during these coordinated intrusions. 

Major retail brands are not alone in facing these vulnerabilities; as noted in ongoing coverage detailing how [Ikea among shops affected by fridge cyber-hacks – Europe live](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/ikea-among-shops-affected-by-fridge-cyber-hacks-europe-live), the attacks exploit connected Internet of Things devices across diverse commercial footprints.

## Assessing the Broader Impact

Modern retail supply chains depend on automated Internet of Things architecture to monitor thousands of inventory points simultaneously, yet this connectivity can create wide attack surfaces for malicious actors. When remote management portals lack robust multi-factor authentication or rely on default administrative credentials, bad actors can easily infiltrate corporate networks. Analysts note that these incidents underscore the hidden vulnerabilities lurking within commercial automation, affecting major retailers, corporate boards, and everyday shoppers who trust supermarket quality controls.

As incident response teams work to secure affected hardware, cybersecurity investigators will likely focus on identifying the specific entry vectors used to access these refrigeration systems. Observers should monitor whether international law enforcement agencies launch a joint task force to track down the perpetrators behind this cross-border digital sabotage campaign.

Sources: [BBC News](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckq6ndq8l6v0o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

articles.aiArticle:
Long before modern endurance racing captured public imagination, massive crowds routinely gathered to watch athletes push the absolute limits of human stamina through long-distance walking, according to a report by **Sport | The Guardian**. 

## The Rise of Pedestrianism and Its Stars

Back when endurance sports held a massive grip on the global sporting consciousness, fans packed venues to witness astonishing feats of physical endurance. The report states that **Edward Payson Weston** stood out as the foremost figure of this era, captivating audiences with his legendary walking exploits. While today's athletic achievements often focus on high-speed sprints or team dominance—much like the incredible milestones seen when [England beat USA to reach World Cup semi-finals](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/england-beat-usa-to-reach-world-cup-semi-finals)—historical sports culture was driven by these grueling, days-long exhibitions of sheer willpower. 

## High Stakes and Extraordinary Regimens

The world surrounding these endurance events was as eccentric as it was demanding. According to the published findings, competitors relied on unusual routines and massive public wagers to fuel their contests. To put the financial scale into perspective, the publication notes a modern parallel: **more than $1.4bn** has been staked on prediction markets for this week’s US midterm elections, according to CNN, illustrating how massive sums of money continue to cluster around high-stakes spectacles. 

*(Context: Long-distance walking, or pedestrianism, originated as a form of messenger travel before evolving into a major spectator sport in the 19th century, frequently drawing tens of thousands of paying spectators to indoor arenas across the United States and Great Britain.)*

## Why This Matters

This look back at pedestrianism highlights how drastically the definition of elite sport has shifted over the past century. For sports historians and modern fans alike, understanding these roots reveals how commercialism, betting, and human endurance have always been deeply intertwined. Just as modern athletes continually push boundaries—such as when elite footballers set new milestones, reflected in our coverage where Drew [Spence 'very proud' to break WSL appearance record](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/spence-very-proud-to-break-wsl-appearance-record)—early pedestrians laid the groundwork for today's massive endurance racing industry. 

## What to Watch

Observers of sports history should watch for renewed academic and cultural interest in forgotten 19th-century pastimes as modern sports platforms dig deeper into archival material. Future retrospectives may uncover further details regarding how these grueling endurance events eventually gave way to motorized racing and modern track and field.

Sources: [Sport | The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/nov/03/pedestrianism-long-distance-walking-edward-payson-weston)

articles.summary: The midterms will shape Congress for the last years of his presidency, writes Sarah Smith, but they are also a test of what politics may look like without him.
articles.content: The midterms will shape Congress for the last years of his presidency, writes Sarah Smith, but they are also a test of what politics may look like without him.
articles.aiArticle:
Voters across the United States are casting their ballots today in high-stakes midterm elections that are poised to dictate the trajectory of Capitol Hill during the final years of the administration. According to reporting by **BBC News**, the legislative contests carry profound implications not only for the remainder of Donald Trump's presidency, but also for the broader direction of the national political arena. 

Midterm elections historically function as a referendum on the sitting occupant of the Oval Office, shifting legislative power and setting hard boundaries on executive authority. As voters head to the voting booths this **November 3**, the composition of the next Congress hangs in the balance, with control of both chambers up for grabs amid an increasingly polarized electorate. 

## Defining the Final Chapter

The stakes of the current legislative cycle extend far beyond routine policy debates on Capitol Hill. Sarah Smith notes in the **BBC News** dispatch that these midterms will fundamentally shape the legislative branch for the remaining years of Trump's presidency. Beyond immediate governance, the contest serves as an early indicator of how the domestic political apparatus will function once the current era concludes. Analysts and observers are closely monitoring whether the outcomes will validate the administration's aggressive agenda or trigger a significant legislative gridlock. This election cycle unfolds against a backdrop of sweeping foreign policy shifts, such as recent [US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-strikes-iranian-island-ahead-of-midterm-elections), alongside intense domestic legal battles that have seen the [Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/supreme-court-rejects-trump-s-request-to-stop-california-counting-disputed-votes). Meanwhile, the administration's economic maneuvers continue to ripple outward, including plans where [Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/supreme-court-rejects-trump-s-request-to-stop-california-counting-disputed-votes).

## Why This Matters

Midterm elections fundamentally alter the balance of power in Washington, serving as the primary check on presidential overreach. For ordinary citizens, the results dictate federal spending priorities, regulatory oversight, and the confirmation of judicial nominees. When a presidency enters its final stretch, congressional majorities hold the leverage to either advance a lame-duck agenda or stall executive initiatives entirely, making every single seat contested today vital for the nation's governance.

## What to Watch

As precincts close across the country, attention will immediately shift to key swing districts and Senate races that historically determine congressional majorities. Observers will be tracking turnout numbers, early voting margins, and how postal ballots are processed in competitive states.

articles.title: Lords of Serendipity by Randy Boyagoda review – a campus satire for this moment of crisis
articles.summary: This propulsive, globe-trotting tale brilliantly skewers the corruption and corporatisation of higher education It’s no secret that academia is on the blink; Canadian author Randy Boyagoda’s new novel, which is equal parts satire, dystopia and exposé, tells…
articles.content: This propulsive, globe-trotting tale brilliantly skewers the corruption and corporatisation of higher education It’s no secret that academia is on the blink; Canadian author Randy Boyagoda’s new novel, which is equal parts satire, dystopia and exposé, tells the story of all that’s wrong, glitchy and broken. Set across Sri Lanka, the United States and Italy, it centres on a cast of students, parents and professors, and their dealings with a common antagonist: the university. The first character we meet is Sri Lankan teen Devi, who is set on obtaining offers from “Ochpys” – her acronym for Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Princeton, Yale and Stanford. To help her realise her dream, Devi’s family of modest means – her mother, father, maternal grandmother and two brothers – hire themselves out as mourners at the funerals of the wealthy. Most of this money goes towards paying Johannes, her tutor on WhatsApp who, unbeknown to Devi, is a hard-up Indian student at Arcadia Tech, an undistinguished university in the US. Meanwhile, Jack, a statistician at the same institution, has taken on an additional teaching load to meet the fees of the elite college his daughter Katrina attends in New England. Soon he catches on to a grade-fixing scheme aimed at flailing international students, run by his teaching assistant Allard Hamburger. Jack is left in disbelief when, to buy his silence, the university puts him on paid administrative leave instead of launching an inquiry into a scandal that has left one student dead by suicide. articles.title: Widening inequality, stagnant pay – Britain urgently needs Labour’s hard-won workers’ rights | Polly Toynbee
articles.summary: The British Social Attitudes survey reveals record levels of dissatisfaction. But still Kemi Badenoch and the business lobby want to take us backwards Britain is unhappier at work than since records began. The British Social Attitudes survey , the nation’s…
articles.content: The British Social Attitudes survey reveals record levels of dissatisfaction. But still Kemi Badenoch and the business lobby want to take us backwards Britain is unhappier at work than since records began. The British Social Attitudes survey , the nation’s long-running annual pulse-taker, finds growing job dissatisfaction in its report, published today. People complain of a lack of flexibility in working hours, a lack of career advancement – and, of course, a lack of pay rises. Who is surprised? Pay stagnation over the last decade is unprecedented since Napoleonic times, the economist Paul Johnson told me, but then corrected himself: “You might as well say ever.” Worse, over the last year pay inequality has jumped up for the first time in a decade, says the Resolution Foundation’s Mike Brewer. Pay for the top 10% rose by 7.3% but only by 1.1% for the bottom 10%. Why? The national living wage has stopped rising faster than median pay, and top pay has taken off again. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘At my age, I can rant!’ Bernie Taupin on Elton John, hellraising vampires and competing in full-blown rodeos
articles.summary: He is the outstanding lyricist who propelled the Rocket Man to 300m sales. As Taupin releases a wistfully grouchy solo album, he talks about the joy of anonymity, his LA drinking gang – and owning a prize-winning bucking bull Bernie Taupin has an interesting…
articles.content: He is the outstanding lyricist who propelled the Rocket Man to 300m sales. As Taupin releases a wistfully grouchy solo album, he talks about the joy of anonymity, his LA drinking gang – and owning a prize-winning bucking bull Bernie Taupin has an interesting take on the strange brand of fame he enjoys. “I am,” he says, “what I call the credit card guy.” I’m sorry? You’re the what? “The credit card guy. I go somewhere, like a shop or a restaurant, and it’s fine. I can be me, no one notices. Then I pay with my credit card and they see the name and go” – he lets out a mock gasp – “‘You’re that guy!’ And I’m the luckiest man in the world in regards to that. I absolutely, positively, 100% love my anonymity, the fact I can walk down the street. I mean, even my contemporaries, people I know – I find I have to introduce myself to them. I was at the Americanafest in Nashville recently and Robert Plant was playing. I hadn’t seen him in years and he said he wanted to meet up. So I walked towards him and there’s that look: ‘Oh God, who the hell’s this?’ ‘Hey, Robert, it’s Bernie!’ ‘Oh my gosh!’ And the next night, we had dinner together.” It’s a neat summation of the curious situation Taupin finds himself in. He is half of one of the most successful songwriting partnerships in history: not all the songs on the 300m records Elton John has sold feature Taupin’s lyrics, but the vast majority do. Furthermore, Taupin has never been an invisible presence in the duo. There’s a photo of him on the sleeve of virtually all of John’s most famous albums: on 1975’s Rock of the Westies, he’s resplendent in a quite extraordinary pair of fringed leather chaps and a shirt open to the navel. Continue reading...

articles.aiArticle:
Financial markets are bracing for a potential monetary policy shift as the **Reserve Bank of Australia** prepares to deliver its latest cash rate decision on **Tuesday**. According to reporting by **World news | The Guardian**, the central bank is anticipated to push borrowing costs to an **18-year high**. 

If enacted, this upcoming decision would mark the **fifth rate hike** implemented by the central bank this year, continuing a persistent tightening cycle aimed at cooling economic pressures. 

## Political Pressures and Budget Questions

Alongside the central bank's imminent monetary announcement, federal politics has grown tense over government fiscal strategy. According to the report from **World news | The Guardian**, questions have been raised regarding whether the ruling Labor administration can guarantee that net savings will not be uncovered during the upcoming mid-year budget update. 

Central banks globally wield benchmark interest rates as their primary monetary policy instrument to manage inflation and stabilize domestic currency value, directly influencing commercial lending rates for mortgages and business loans. 

## Why This Matters

As borrowing costs climb to levels not seen in nearly two decades, household budgets across the country face mounting pressure. Higher interest rates typically translate into heavier monthly mortgage repayments, squeezing discretionary spending and dampening consumer demand. Property markets frequently bear the brunt of these tightening cycles, as seen in broader trends where [home values fall for seventh consecutive month as interest rates dent demand](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/home-values-fall-for-seventh-consecutive-month-as-interest-rates-dent-demand), forcing prospective buyers and current owners to reevaluate their financial commitments. 

Beyond domestic shores, similar economic headwinds are affecting borrowers internationally, leaving [millions in UK brace to remortgage on worse deals as rate rise looms](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/millions-in-uk-brace-to-remortgage-on-worse-deals-as-rate-rise).

## What to Watch

articles.content: US government agencies and cyber analysts have blamed Pyongyang for the record-breaking heist.
articles.aiArticle:
Pyongyang has formally rejected accusations that it engineered the unprecedented **$6.3bn** cryptocurrency theft from **Binance**, pushing back against allegations leveled by American authorities and digital security researchers. According to **BBC News**, the state-backed denial arrives in the wake of mounting international scrutiny linking state-sponsored hacking syndicates in North Korea to the massive breach. 

The security breach stands as the largest digital asset heist in history, shaking confidence across the digital finance sector. In the immediate aftermath, exchange operators scrambled to reassure users, with executives reporting that the platform has secured coverage for **90%** of the stolen funds. As detailed in our previous reporting on how **[Binance says 90% of losses from $6.3bn hack covered as FBI says North Korea behind attack](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/binance-says-of-losses-from-bn-hack-covered-as-fbi-says-north)**, federal investigators immediately pointed fingers at eastern state actors. Additional background on the mechanics of the digital security breach is available through our coverage examining how **[North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/north-korea-linked-to-massive-binance-crypto-heist)**.

## Conflicting Claims and Official Stances

United States government bodies, alongside independent cyber intelligence investigators cited by **BBC News**, maintain that Pyongyang orchestrated the security penetration. These analytical groups point to established patterns of state-directed financial cybercrime designed to evade economic sanctions. Conversely, North Korean officials have dismissed these assertions entirely, characterizing the allegations as fabricated propaganda intended to damage the nation's reputation. 

Cryptocurrency heists have increasingly become a primary method for sanctioned regimes to acquire foreign currency, bypassing traditional banking restrictions through decentralized finance networks. Cybersecurity experts note that tracing stolen digital tokens through blockchain mixers presents immense technical hurdles for international law enforcement agencies. Consequently, attributing complex breaches to specific nation-states often relies on behavioral analytics and digital signatures rather than direct physical evidence.

## The Stakes and Impact

*Context: Financial security analysts emphasize that multi-billion-dollar exploits pose systemic risks to the broader adoption of blockchain technology and digital asset exchanges. When vulnerabilities of this magnitude are exploited, everyday retail investors face potential losses, while regulatory bodies face intense pressure to impose stricter compliance mandates on trading platforms.*

*What to watch: Observers will be monitoring whether international law enforcement agencies release technical attribution data to substantiate their claims against Pyongyang, as well as how major exchanges adjust their cold-storage security protocols in response.*

Sources: [BBC News](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rey4v53exgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

Five people were being treated in hospital, including two rescue workers. Continue reading...
articles.aiArticle:
A Russian bombing raid targeting an aid distribution point and an adjacent shelter in southern Ukraine has left **at least 26** people dead, according to Ukrainian officials. 

The strike destroyed vital humanitarian infrastructure on **Monday**, prompting sharp condemnation from Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced the assault as a "vile" action, stating that the attack demonstrates Moscow has no genuine interest in de-escalating the ongoing conflict. The facility was actively providing relief to civilians in the southern region when the ordnance hit, devastating both the distribution hub and the nearby refuge used by vulnerable residents.

## Humanitarian Impact and Wider Conflict Context

Targeting civilian relief operations exacerbates the immense suffering endured by populations near the front lines, disrupting the delivery of food, medicine, and shelter materials. This incident unfolds against a backdrop of intensifying hostilities, mirroring patterns seen in earlier attacks such as the [Russian bombing kills 24 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/russian-bombing-kills-people-at-ukraine-aid-centre-kyiv-says). Civilian infrastructure has frequently borne the brunt of military campaigns throughout the war, leaving millions dependent on local aid networks for survival.

As diplomatic efforts stall, military engagements continue to ripple across the energy and civilian sectors, compounding hardships for communities already grappling with power outages, as documented in reports detailing how [Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/russian-strikes-cut-power-to-thousands-in-ukraine-as-kherson-ceasefire-ends). The systematic targeting of non-combatant hubs raises significant concerns regarding adherence to international humanitarian law.

## Why This Matters

Context: The deliberate destruction of humanitarian aid stations strikes directly at the lifeline of populations surviving in active combat zones. When distribution points and shelters are rendered inoperable, local communities lose access to absolute essentials, compounding the human toll of the war far beyond the immediate battlefields. For international observers and donors, these attacks complicate relief logistics and heighten the urgency of securing protected corridors for civilian aid workers and recipients alike.

What to watch: Analysts will monitor whether international bodies issue heightened protective mandates for humanitarian personnel and whether local authorities can establish secure, alternative distribution sites away from vulnerable front-line sectors.

articles.content: A Kyiv startup’s pocket-sized, 10-ounce receiver lets Ukrainian troops watch the video feeds of Russian drones, though Russian moves toward digital video and AI-guided drones that emit no signals could make the victory short-lived.

Ukrainian forces are utilizing a lightweight, portable receiver developed by a local Kyiv startup to intercept and view video feeds broadcast by incoming Russian unmanned aerial vehicles, according to a recent report by **TechCrunch**. Weighing just **10 ounces** and small enough to fit inside a pocket, the equipment gives ground troops immediate visibility into enemy reconnaissance and targeting paths. By tapping into these unsecured video transmissions, defenders can track approaching threats in real time.

## Technological Arms Race on the Frontline

The development highlights the continuous adaptation required on the battlefield, where electronic warfare and aerial scouting dictate the pace of combat. As seen in other theaters of the conflict, such as when [Russian bombing kills 24 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/russian-bombing-kills-people-at-ukraine-aid-centre-kyiv-says), civilian areas and military positions alike face relentless aerial observation. This new receiver offers a tactical countermeasure, allowing soldiers to spot hazards before strikes occur. Even so, the reporting notes that this technological advantage might be temporary. The publication warns that Russian developers are steadily transitioning toward digital video transmissions and artificial intelligence-guided drones that operate without emitting standard radio frequency signals, which would render current interception methods obsolete.

## Strategic Implications and Future Outlook

*(Context: This cat-and-mouse dynamic underscores the relentless technological evolution of modern warfare, where hardware advantages measured in months can completely shift frontline safety margins. For Ukrainian manufacturers and front-line units, staying ahead requires constant software iteration to match enemy counter-measures.)*

*(What to watch: Analysts will be monitoring whether local startups can scale production of these receivers quickly enough before adversaries fully deploy signal-silent, AI-piloted hardware across the entire theater.)*

articles.title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
articles.summary: The men and women who rummage through commercial bins to take clothes and other items.
articles.content: The men and women who rummage through commercial bins to take clothes and other items.
articles.aiArticle:
A growing community of urban scavengers is turning commercial waste containers into a lifeline, rescuing everything from high-end electronics to everyday toiletries and saving hundreds of dollars in the process, according to a recent report by BBC News. 

## The Reality of Commercial Rummaging

BBC News details how dedicated individuals search through the refuse receptacles of major retailers and businesses to retrieve perfectly usable goods destined for landfills. Rather than searching exclusively for discarded food—a practice long associated with urban foraging—these modern scavengers focus on manufactured products. According to the broadcasting network's coverage, participants in this practice regularly unearth brand-new items including electric scooters, clothing, and commercial-grade shampoo still in their original packaging. 

For many people navigating this lifestyle, the motivation stems from a mixture of environmental concern and financial necessity. The report highlights that individuals engaging in bin diving can accumulate hundreds of dollars worth of merchandise simply by monitoring the disposal habits of local commercial establishments. This informal recovery network operates entirely outside standard retail channels, sustained entirely by the volume of goods routinely thrown away by consumer businesses.

## Why This Matters

Urban waste recovery touches on a complex intersection of modern consumer habits, environmental sustainability, and economic pressure. When young people face severe economic hurdles, many find themselves questioning long-term financial stability, sometimes leading them to adopt unconventional coping mechanisms such as [splashing out on the present moment despite a sense that they are doomed anyway](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/we-re-doomed-anyway-young-people-disheartened-about-the-future-are-splashing). Conversely, others turn away from consumerism altogether through dumpster diving, directly highlighting the staggering scale of corporate waste. The practice exposes the vast surplus generated by modern supply chains, where functional items are routinely discarded rather than discounted, donated, or recycled. 

## What to Watch

As municipalities and commercial property owners increasingly crack down on scavenging through security measures and locked enclosures, the future of urban waste recovery remains uncertain. Observers will be monitoring whether retailers face mounting regulatory pressure to curb corporate waste or if local authorities will introduce stricter trespassing enforcement against individuals searching commercial bins. 

Sources: [BBC News](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm86zdp2ygqno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

articles.content: Y Combinator Garry Tan has jokingly admitted that he's suffered from "cyber psychosis” and barely sleeps sometimes because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast, The Builders, Tan put a price tag on his passion.
articles.aiArticle:
Y Combinator leader **Garry Tan** has revealed that his heavy reliance on automated digital assistants costs him as much as **$200,000 annually** just in computing tokens, according to a recent interview. Speaking on Walter Isaacson’s podcast *The Builders*, Tan half-jokingly described his immersive workflow as a form of "cyber psychosis" that occasionally robs him of sleep due to sheer excitement over what artificial intelligence can accomplish. 

The conversation sheds light on the extreme edge of personal productivity tooling among Silicon Valley executives. While most professionals utilize automated models for basic correspondence or light drafting, Tan's massive expenditure highlights a lifestyle deeply intertwined with autonomous digital workers. 

## The High Cost of Autonomous Workflows

According to TechCrunch, Tan broke down his staggering financial commitment to these computational resources during his appearance on the podcast. Running continuous loops of automated tasks and multi-step reasoning models demands immense processing power, driving his annual token bill up to the **$200,000** threshold. 

This financial footprint reflects a broader shift in how industry leaders interact with software, moving from passive tools to active, autonomous agents that execute complex operations. As hardware demands shift across the tech sector, companies are also managing complex supply chains, much like how manufacturing pressures impact hardware makers dealing with [soaring inventory and memory chip costs](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/apple-s-inventory-surges-as-memory-chip-costs-climb) amid broader market changes.

## Why This Matters

Tan's experience offers a window into the potential future of executive productivity, but it also underscores widening disparities in how software is utilized. For early adopters with deep capital reserves, dropping six figures on computing tokens enables superhuman output and round-the-clock operations. However, this level of dependency raises questions about burnout, cognitive load, and the sustainability of human-machine integration in leadership roles. 

Beyond individual habits, such heavy usage strains underlying infrastructure, feeding continuous demand for massive data centers and specialized silicon. These infrastructure bottlenecks echo the supply hurdles seen in consumer hardware, where manufacturers admit it remains [hard to predict when supply constraints will improve](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/apple-says-it-s-hard-to-predict-when-iphone-duo-constraints-will) for high-demand devices. 

## What to Watch

Observers should monitor whether enterprise pricing structures adapt to accommodate heavy individual power users or if token costs remain a prohibitive luxury for standard operations. As autonomous assistants become more capable, the boundary between executive oversight and algorithmic delegation will continue to blur.

Sources: [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/02/y-combinators-garry-tan-uses-ai-agents-so-much-he-spends-up-to-200k-a-year-on-tokens/)

articles.content: Julian Fellowes’ high-society period drama has, somehow, picked up Emmys and reached its fourth series. Poor Meryl Streep must feel so awkward watching her daughter Louisa Jacobson in such a uniformly awful show A doctor with a fully qualified moustache races up a carriageway towards an immaculate stately home. “I fear we should have sent for you sooner!” says the lady who greets him on the doorstep as the screams of a woman in drug-free labour rattle the windows in their frames. Oh, ya think? is not Dr Moustache’s reply. When this many cliches assemble so quickly, it can only mean one thing: Brownstone Abbey – AKA Julian Fellowes’ Revenge, AKA What Did We Do to Deserve This?, AKA The Gilded Age if you insist on its official title – is back for a fourth and, no one has said let alone promised, final season. articles.title: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
articles.summary: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Whether you intend to put its many tracking features to the test, or you simply want the longest battery life of any Apple Watch, it’s currently on sale for $699.99 ($100 off) in multiple…
articles.content: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Whether you intend to put its many tracking features to the test, or you simply want the longest battery life of any Apple Watch, it’s currently on sale for $699.99 ($100 off) in multiple colors at Amazon , matching its all-time low price. Apple Watch Ultra 4 Where to Buy: $799 $699 at Amazon Powered by Apple’s new S11 chip (also in the Series 12), the Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers faster performance than the last-gen version, plus a handful of new Apple Intelligence features. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. An upcoming Siri Recap feature will be able to create summaries of conversations for later reference. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12 . Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon , just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot . The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off) , while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off) . You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off) . Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon . The versatile tool can help with repairing stuff, or putting together decorations. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it. The stapler comes with 1,200 fasteners.

articles.content: Credit to Arsenal for restricting opportunities at Anfield but Iraola will need his side to learn to unpick low backlines Liverpool did not have a shot on target in their 1-0 defeat by Arsenal on Sunday, according to Opta, the first time they have drawn this type of blank in a Premier League game at Anfield since records began in 2003-04. They did not find the target in a goalless draw at the Emirates Stadium this year either, though in both games they struck the woodwork. The margins tend to be fine when recording statistical outliers. If Alexis Mac Allister’s floated ball from distance into David Raya’s waiting arms had actually counted as a shot, would Andoni Iraola’s side have delivered a markedly better attacking performance? Far more concerning for the Spaniard will be that his team had 52 touches in the Arsenal penalty area (which is good) to create only one Opta‑defined big chance (which is bad). The Premier League average this season is five times more efficient; 10.3 box touches per big chance. Continue reading...

articles.title: Russian bombing kills 24 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
articles.summary: Local officials say 27 people had been missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit a village in southern Ukraine.
articles.content: Local officials say 27 people had been missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit a village in southern Ukraine.
articles.aiArticle:
At least **24 people** have been killed following a devastating Russian bombing raid that targeted a humanitarian aid distribution hub in southern Ukraine, according to statements released by Kyiv officials. BBC News reports that the deadly barrage involved a staggering deployment of heavy ordnance, flattening the rural location where civilians gathered for assistance. 

## Scale of Destruction and Missing Persons

According to local authorities cited by BBC News, the attack saw the deployment of at least **nine 3,000kg aerial bombs** dropped directly onto the village settlement. The massive concussive force of the high-payload munitions left behind catastrophic structural damage and deep craters at the distribution point. In the immediate aftermath of the strike, regional administrators confirmed that **27 people** remained unaccounted for as rescue crews scrambled to sift through the heavily compressed rubble. articles.content: The final day of the regular season gave fans Gotham’s Shield win, a farewell to a Seattle hero and a new part-whiparound, part-watchalong show to take it all in As a player, Ali Krieger went into NWSL Decision Day focused on one result. She was Gotham FC’s captain in 2023, the first time the league played all of the final games of the regular season simultaneously. The job, she remembers, was to not worry about the other games going on. Three years later, Krieger spent Decision Day with eyes on not one game but eight. For the first time, all of the final games of the NWSL season were aired by the same network. Krieger, now a lead analyst for ESPN, and host Kelsey Riggs Cuff anchored the coverage from headquarters in Bristol with a show that was part whiparound, part watchalong, and ultimately wholly new for the 14-year-old league. In the meantime, though, here’s a thumping profits warning from Ibstock, the country’s biggest brickmaker, to spread a little more gloom. Demand hit a brick wall in the summer, as the company could have put it. Industry data, said Ibstock , show UK brick market volumes down 17% year-on-year in July and August. articles.title: Why Peacock is making a huge bet on YouTube
articles.summary: Today, I’m talking with Matt Strauss, who is now chairman of the NBCUniversal Media Group. This is Matt’s second time joining me on the show, and there’s been a whole lot of organizational and structural change at NBCU since the last time he and I spoke just…
articles.content: Today, I’m talking with Matt Strauss, who is now chairman of the NBCUniversal Media Group. This is Matt’s second time joining me on the show, and there’s been a whole lot of organizational and structural change at NBCU since the last time he and I spoke just two years ago — pure Decoder bait. First, about a month after Matt was on the show, Comcast spun off most of the NBCU cable channels into something called Versant. That’s when Matt’s title changed from heading up just the direct-to-consumer offering — meaning Peacock, plus some other streaming services — to heading up the whole thing, across all distribution. And now, Comcast is spinning off the NBCU business entirely into a whole new standalone company. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . That’s a lot to have going on all at once! And meanwhile, it’s only just this year that Peacock became an actual profitable business at all — and it’s still pretty far away from being anything like the juggernaut that Netflix is. But what NBCU has, and what Peacock has, that the rest of the streaming industry is still trying to wrap its head around, is live sports. Sports are huge. They held up the cable industry for years, they held up broadcast, and now they’re the big thing that could make streaming a winner for NBC. One thing before we start: You’ll hear me ask Matt about the red company and the blue company. That’s just my way of getting Matt to talk about Netflix and Skydance, the company that now owns both Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. I think he did a good job playing along. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Matt Strauss, chairman of the NBCU Media Group. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Matt Strauss, you are the chairman of the NBCUniversal Media Group. Welcome back to Decoder . Thank you so much, Nilay. It’s great to be back. I am very excited to talk to you. There’s a lot going on in the media. It is a tumultuous time in Hollywood. I have to tell the audience that you and I are speaking minutes after Anthropic filed its S-1 , and all of humanity is going to be turned into AI. Who knows what entertainment we’ll be watching in the future? There’s a lot going on. Let’s start at the very beginning of this. You have a new job since last time you were on the show. Last time, you were the head of Direct-to-Consumer — you were basically the head of Peacock and the other apps inside the family. Now you’re the chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group. What’s the new job? What does that mean? NBCUniversal Media Group is comprised of certain services within NBC. It’s the broadcast network, it’s Bravo, it’s Peacock, it’s NBC Sports. We also have NBC News and Telemundo. One of the things that we recognized, especially when we spun off some of our cable assets last year into Versant, was that the assets we had truly worked better together. NBC has been like a megaphone. Given the reach of NBC, it’s been incredibly strategic in growing Peacock, which is a bit ironic because I think so many people believed that broadcasting was a bit of a relic of the past in this digital world, but it’s actually proven to be the opposite. As things have gotten more fragmented, having a broadcast network is actually a superpower because we’re continuing to see ratings growth. That has been really helpful as we’ve been building out Peacock. But actually, Peacock was also finding new audiences, like cord cutters or people who maybe didn’t grow up watching NBC or some of our cable networks. So, Peacock’s also been really strategic in reaching and driving people back to NBC and Bravo. So, I think that flywheel is where we recognized that we needed to start operating differently. I’ve been a huge advocate of what I like to call “centers of excellence” in how I like to structure the business, which is, content first and platform second. How do we get maximum reach, maximum engagement? That really required us thinking differently about how we were running the business. Essentially, instead of having a programming group within broadcast and a programming group within streaming, we just collapsed the business. Now you’ve got one programming team, one marketing team, one product and technology team, one decision sciences and research team, and one advertising team. They’re all incentivized around continuing to grow the portfolio, get that maximum reach, maximum engagement, and drive top-line revenue. I think that structure, which we put in place about 18 months ago, is contributing to a lot of the success that we’re seeing now. Even if you look at 2026, NBC is the number one network in total viewers. We had an unbelievable early part of the year with “Legendary February,” which you might remember. That’s when we had the Super Bowl, the Milan Cortina Olympics, and the NBA All-Star Game. In 17 days, we reached over 225 million viewers. This summer, we had Love Island , which was the number one show of the summer for streaming. You had the World Cup, which was the number one Spanish-language sporting event in US history on Telemundo and Peacock. We had a show called The Five-Star Weekend , which was our number one scripted drama. Now, we’ve led ourselves into the fall, where we have Sunday Night Football, which has been the number one show for 15 consecutive years. We had a great kickoff with over 25 million viewers. We just had the NBA tip-off last week with the Knicks and the Sixers, which is the number one rated tip-off in NBA history. So, it does feel like we’re firing on all cylinders in how we’re trying to operate with this, again, content-first-platform-second mantra. But just to go one level deeper, a big part of this strategy is figuring out how do we move audiences across platforms. For example, when I mentioned that Love Island was the number one streaming show of the summer, 40 percent of those Love Island viewers also tuned in to watch the World Cup. So, migrating viewers back and forth across the portfolio is a critical part of how we see ourselves continuing to grow. But to effectuate that, you need to structure yourself in a way where people are incentivized along that vision. We’re still evolving as an organization, but I’m really proud of some of the milestones and accomplishments that we’ve made as a team. I love my job. I feel like I’ve got the best job in the industry at the moment. It is a tumultuous time in Hollywood, and you seem like one of the happiest people in the industry right at the second. That is very notable. You’re a Decoder pro, you brought up structure. I’m dying to ask you about the Decision Sciences Group. That’s the other question I ask everybody. But let me just back out for one second. You’re describing quite a lot of freedom in rethinking how something like NBCUniversal would work. You mentioned the Versant spin, so CNBC, MS Now, and a bunch of channels went that way. I’m on its networks all the time. I would describe the folks at Versant as feeling more free. They’re disconnected from the battleship that was Comcast and NBCUniversal. They can go try whatever they want to try. They’re energized by it in some ways. Then, Comcast looked at NBCUniversal and said, “We’re going to spin off that off as well. We’re going to be the cable business and NBCUniversal will be the entertainment business, and now you’re in charge of that.” You’re like a 20-year Comcast veteran. I think you got your start doing cable boxes. Yep. I started in 2004 at Comcast. Just tell me about that process. We spun off CNBC and MS Now into Versant. Now we’re looking at this company. We ought to spin off NBCUniversal as well. Just tell me about how that came about. What was that moment like? Did you all sit in a boardroom? Did it come down from on high? How did that happen? Well, that decision really was made by Brian Roberts and Mike Cavanagh. Candidly, I was not in the room when that decision was made, but I think if you were to ask people at NBCUniversal, it makes strategic sense. Do you feel that same sense of freedom? You know what? I think that there’s an energy. When people show up here, they feel very passionate about what they do. They believe in our strategy, they believe in our portfolio. Look at NBCUniversal more broadly. Before, I was describing the Media Group, but that is one piece of the broader company. You have Universal Pictures and Universal Television, which have obviously been having an unbelievable summer with The Odyssey and Obsession . You’ve got Universal’s theme parks and experiences. We opened up Epic Universe last year. We opened up a kids theme park in Texas. We announced we’re going to open up a theme park in the UK . We have Sky, which was part of the company but more squarely sat within Comcast Cable. Now that’s going to migrate over to the new NBCUniversal as part of this restructure. Then, you have these media assets, which I spoke about earlier. So, you’ve got this unbelievable portfolio. I think that people here really believe in our growth and that if we’re a separate company, it’s going to allow us to move faster. It’s going to let us have more clarity around where we want to make capital allocations and decisions. There are a few areas that really play to our strengths as an organization. One of them is live sports and live events. That’s always been a part of NBCUniversal that we’re really known for. If you just look at the sports portfolio that we have, Nilay, we’ve got NFL, NBA, MLB, the Big Ten Conference, the Premier League. We’ve got the Olympics with the IOC. You’ve got this unbelievable portfolio of sports content, and that’s a strategic asset when we’re partnering with the leagues because we believe in broadcast. We believe in broad reach. We’re not trying to put everything exclusively on a streaming platform. In 2026, we’ve demonstrated across almost every single sport that we can actually continue to grow ratings and reach new audiences, which is something that’s becoming more and more complicated. Can I ask about that? Because you also run Peacock, which is a paid streamer where you can access sports. When you say grow ratings on broadcast, are more people putting up antennas to watch sports over the air? No. What I mean… By the way, about 20 percent of TV households in this country do still use over-the-air antennas as— Oh, we have lots of listeners who are going to tell you that’s the best picture quality you can get. Yeah. It is amazing picture quality, especially if you live in the right look angle where you could pick up the signal. It comes back to what I said earlier about managing as a portfolio. We don’t think of it as a broadcast business sitting next to a streaming business. We really position ourselves as a digital-first company trying to get that maximum reach. When we look at the ratings, we’re combining what you would think of as more traditional ratings for linear television with streaming and all of our digital platforms. Whether that’s DVR or TV Everywhere, we aggregate it into one platform. When you look at it through that lens, which is just audience, we’ve actually demonstrated that across almost every sport — NFL, NBA, or MLB — the total viewers that we are reaching now are, in some cases, the highest they’ve been in decades. Even the Super Bowl, which we had earlier this year on NBC, reached about 137 million viewers at its peak, and that’s across all of our platforms. That Super Bowl was the highest-rated live event in NBC’s 100-year anniversary, which is this year. It’s kind of counterintuitive, but what we’re showing is that when we start operating as one, we can reach new audiences and we can aggregate them. We are demonstrating that not just across sports. There’s even something like the Thanksgiving Day Parade, which has been an institution on NBC for 99 years. This past Thanksgiving Day Parade was the highest-rated parade we have had in the company’s history. So, there’s a renaissance happening around live. In a world of instant gratification, on demand, and watching what you want when you want, the fact that you’re now seeing more and more viewers wanting the collective consciousness of social viewing, things that still matter in today’s society, that actually plays to our strengths. And we’re seeing that manifest itself with higher ratings. But as I mentioned, it’s also a big part of our strategy. It was a big part of our Peacock strategy, which was a bit of an anomaly when we launched Peacock six years ago. It’s also a huge part of what I think NBC does well, which is that we create these big tentpole events and we’re able to shine a light on them and get huge audiences that are continuing to show up, even in a world of fragmentation and cord-cutting. It’s interesting that you’ve described it as content first and platform second, and then you’re describing your approach to ratings as agnostic to distribution. You’re just sort of combining everything and saying, “This is the number of people we reached.” Well, take something like the Milan Cortina Olympics. This is an interesting example. If you were to look at that Winter Olympics, we had roughly 3,200 hours of content. There’s no way we can make all of that available on one network. There’s no way to daypart 3,200 hours. If you remember what we did with the Paris Olympics, we made the decision to make every event available live. When you make it all available live, we put it all on Peacock. This was a very controversial decision because the question has always historically been that if people tune in to watch this live during the day on Peacock, are they going to tune in to watch NBC primetime? Are we going to cannibalize our ratings or are we going to grow the ratings? This is where we really tested this strategy. If we’re truly indifferent, then what should happen is that we should be able to expand the funnel during the day, get more people into the Olympics, and try to create an experience that we’re very proud of. We really do believe, whether it was the Gold Zone or Multiview, that we were able to surprise and delight viewers and make it really easy to navigate and find all of the choices on Peacock. But then what happened was that people were tuning in to watch NBC during primetime because there’s a difference between what NBC does and what Peacock does. NBC was more about storytelling. It was more about, “Let’s talk about what happened today. What about the backstory of the athletes? How’s Mike Tirico going to address his perspective on things?” When you combine these two things together — putting all the content on Peacock and then having the primetime show — this Winter Olympics had about a 96 percent higher rating. About 25 million viewers were tuning in to watch the Milan Cortina Olympics, which was about 96 or 97 percent higher than Beijing. On the digital side, it was double the digital minutes of every other Winter Olympics combined. We also doubled the advertising revenue. You’ve got to be willing to break some glass. This is going to seem so obvious, but it starts with the consumer. It starts with, “How do we approach the consumer and give them the best experience?” And if you build it, they will come. The only reason I’m using the Olympics as an example is because if you were to look at the past, this was a real pain point where we didn’t make everything available on streaming or it was confusing for some viewers to figure out how to navigate all of the choices. We really, as an organization, decided to put our shoulder behind this, and I think the results ultimately speak for themselves. But again, it ladders back up to this vision of really starting to manage as one portfolio. If you can drive that maximum reach and engagement, that’s also going to be where you’ll get the best monetization. The Verge team in particular was addicted to Gold Zone , which was the whip-around coverage of every medal event. It was very fun. Let me ask you about this. A big Decoder trope is that your distribution fundamentally affects what you make, right? That the medium is essentially the message, and I know what a YouTuber makes because they’re on YouTube, and I know what a TikToker makes because they’re on TikTok. I could stretch this all the way back and say I know what broadcast TV looks like because the medium of broadcast TV has fundamentally shaped the content that gets made there. I know what cable shows on Bravo look like, and they’re not the same thing and they haven’t been for a while. You’re describing, “We’re going to bring programming in, we’re going to centralize that, we’re going to be agnostic to distribution — or indifferent I think is the word you used — and that’s going to increase viewership.” But the pressure of the different distributions is still there, right? Running the broadcast network over the air is still different and reaches different people than distributing on YouTube TV, than running Peacock as a paid platform unto itself. How do you manage that tension? Because it is real. Yeah, it is very real. It’s a really insightful question. The tension is real, but actually, I don’t view it as tension. I view it as an opportunity because you’ve got different audiences. If it’s a Venn diagram and you look at who’s the audience on broadcast versus the audience on cable versus the audience on streaming, there’s some overlap, but it’s not as much as you would think. That actually speaks to this broader strategy, which is, “How do we reach?” If we reach all these different viewers but they’re on different platforms, how do we start bringing this together into one? Now there’s multiple ways to effectuate that kind of a strategy. One is you start sharing content and window content differently across platforms. For example, we have a show on Peacock called The Paper . Greg Daniels created it, who also created The Office . It’s a really great comedy and it’s an original. If you were to look at how streaming services typically make originals available, they’re exclusive. You premiere it on your streaming platform, and it typically stays on that platform forever. What we’re starting to experiment with is, well, what if we premiere The Paper on Peacock but then introduce it onto NBC six months later? Now you’re bringing a show that was created for streaming and making it available on NBC to a new audience. You also have this added message, which is that if you want to watch next week’s episode now, go get Peacock. All of a sudden, NBC is not only reaching new audiences but it’s also becoming a sales channel for driving people back to sign up for Peacock. Do you give that to Greg Daniels? The feedback loop of a YouTuber is so blunt. I’ve made a handful of Instagram Reels in my life. I literally open and look at the retention chart and think, “Oh, I should put another hook in there in the middle to keep my viewers,” and it’s immediate. That’s not even how my brain works. It’s immediate that the data makes you think this way. If you say to Greg Daniels, “Hey, make sure episode two of The Office ends on a cliffhanger so that I can advertise watching the next episode right away on Peacock. Well, Donna Langley, who oversees all of the entertainment programming, would be the one calling Greg Daniels and giving him that feedback. But here would be a different way to answer that question. I don’t think we’re necessarily trying to change the framework of how some of the shows are being created on NBC or Peacock. There’s still something about premium content and how that’s being created that I think resonates with a lot of people. But here’s what we’re thinking differently. Take a show like Saturday Night Live. We had the 50-year anniversary for SNL a couple of years ago, and it’s unbelievable what Lorne Michaels has created. You still have SNL that’s on at 11:30PM ET, but what if we now take that content and we format it for vertical video on Peacock? We know that there’s a whole cohort of people that are watching on their phone, holding it vertically, and likely using their forefinger or their thumb to navigate because of TikTok or Reels. You’ve brought me to the other Decoder question. I think you’ve talked a lot about structure already. The other question I ask everybody is how they make decisions. We’ve got an unbelievable team, in my opinion, that has created a best-in-class, scalable platform that not only powers Peacock, but also powers Sky’s Now TV. It’s the same platform that we’ve also distributed to dozens of countries around the world. We’ve got a world-class team that is really trying to transform, surprise, and delight viewers in a way that I’m not sure other platforms are going to be able to do around our content and franchises, especially when it comes to especially these major tentpole events. I want to end by asking maybe the most important question of all. We’re talking a lot about internet-distributed businesses and consumers signing up for services and being able to churn and quit. There are a lot of free market dynamics there, which I think are very powerful and very important. That means you get to program whatever you want to program. You have chosen live in sports and, importantly, you mentioned news at the top of this conversation. NBC News is part of this portfolio. NBC News is also distributed over broadcast. It’s distributed over the air. The Trump administration and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, in particular, has expressed a lot of desire to pressure broadcast networks because you use the public spectrum, particularly news networks. He’s withheld the broadcast licenses for ABC stations, for example. He has threatened the other broadcast networks. There’s a lot of pressure on NBC News. How are you handling that? Are you pushing back? Because that is the one place where you’re not allowed to just do whatever you want, right? The government gets to tell you what to say in an increasingly uncomfortable way. Yeah. Look, I think I give a lot of credit to [NBCUniversal News Group Chairman] Cesar Conde and the NBC News organization who are big believers in freedom of speech and freedom of the press. I think they’re doing a fantastic job. When it comes to distribution of our content, especially our news programming, I think that’s an example where it’s available everywhere. I mean, we truly make it available not only on Peacock, NBC, and over the air, but through Fast TV, NBC News Now— Have you made this argument to the administration? Because I’ve met a lot of FCC chairmen over the years, and until Carr showed up, the argument they would make is that we have to get away from overthinking broadcast because the audience is everywhere, and they don’t actually make a distinction between broadcast television and cable. That was a Republican talking point for years and years. This is nonsense. The other version is that everyone’s on TikTok and the industry has to contend with that in some way. We should get more people internet access because that will actually even the playing field. Now we’ve come to, “You have to use the spectrum in the public interest.” It is different and the government should impose some speech pressure — which again, I think is inappropriate — but that is a new argument. I’m wondering if you have said to the administration, “Look, the consumer doesn’t make this distinction and we as a company aren’t making this distinction.” Well, I’ve not had those direct conversations myself. Obviously, we have a government affairs team that works very closely with regulators in DC. There’s probably no better time to be alive than right now when it comes to being able to access content through multiple modalities, whether it’s over-the-air broadcast, social media platforms, or free. If you were to look at Peacock, not only do we distribute NBC News, we distribute all of our own stations as well. I could be watching the Los Angeles local news in New York or I could be watching the Philadelphia local news. There’s no shortage of ways that we are supporting the public good in giving them multiple ways and choices in how they want to consume and access their news programming, and I don’t think that’s going to change. I think we’re going to continue to advocate for freedom of speech and freedom of the press. I think our news organization has been doing an unbelievable job in the product and the service that they’re doing for the public. Yeah. Matt, you can tell that’s an important topic for me for a lot of reasons. What’s next for NBCUniversal Media Group? What’s next for Peacock? What should people be looking for? I think what’s next for NBCUniversal Media Group is, as we talked about, we will likely be a separate company as part of the new NBC this time next year. You’ve got to come back. There’s a bunch of questions where I knew I wasn’t going to get answers because the deal isn’t closed yet. When that closes, you’ve got to come back because I have a million questions. I will definitely come back. I’m really looking forward to it. I think the other piece, as you know, is that we had our Q3 earnings last week. We talked a lot about Peacock and how we had a very different strategy with Peacock from the others when we launched our service six years ago. I’m really proud to share that Peacock was profitable in Q3 for the second consecutive quarter. We had $261 million of EBITDA. That’s $470 million better year-over-year. I think the team has done an unbelievable job, and I feel really good about our momentum and continuing to grow. It’s good proof that there’s not one way to go to market. There’s not one strategy or approach. You’ve got to play your hand and to your strengths, and you’re going to see us continue to do that at NBCUniversal. Yeah. We didn’t even talk about what AI might do to the cost structure of video. When you come back, we’re going to get into it. Matt, thank you so much for being on Decoder . Thank you so much. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

articles.summary: I thought the explanation I’d given about black holes was family-friendly; but after what she had said, I had to rethink my examples Read more in the a job that changed me series In the first year of my science degree, I was fortunate to land a job as an…
articles.content: I thought the explanation I’d given about black holes was family-friendly; but after what she had said, I had to rethink my examples Read more in the a job that changed me series In the first year of my science degree, I was fortunate to land a job as an astronomy guide at the Sydney Observatory. In my role, I would lead tour groups of about 20 people. We’d look at stars and planets through telescopes. If the skies were filled from horizon to horizon with clouds, we’d explore more of the universe through a 3D theatre. And to peer beyond what our telescopes could see, we’d pile inside the cosy planetarium, seeing what the light pollution of Sydney and clouds would often obstruct from our view. My favourite object to show in the planetarium was the Hubble Ultra Deep Field image. Before revealing the image, I’d explain how the Hubble space telescope had stared at a piece of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm’s length for 11 days, collecting enough light to look into the farthest corners of the universe. Then I’d zoom in on that tiny piece of sky, revealing the gorgeous image. At least one person would audibly gasp at the reveal. Continue reading...

articles.content: Many treatments are now extending lives, but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve Two decades ago, a dear friend called me in a trembling voice. Was there hope for his young nephew , whose cancer had spread to the brain? Sadly, “no”, I said. But today, for such patients, there are options that were unimaginable back then. Recently, researchers at the European Society For Medical Oncology presented the latest chapter results from a randomised controlled trial of a bespoke cancer vaccine for patients with high-risk melanoma. The trial involved 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but remained at high recurrence risk. They received either pembrolizumab, an established immunotherapy, or pembrolizumab combined with an experimental mRNA vaccine, designed to help the immune system recognise and attack targets unique to the patient’s tumour. articles.content: Prospect to hold workplace sessions and recruit members under agreement with tech company Trade unions are expected to make further inroads into big tech companies in the UK after new rights for unions to access workplaces came into force , with Google UK signing an agreement on Monday. The Prospect union has reached an agreement with Google to begin organising among about 7,000 workers across its UK operations, including YouTube but excluding DeepMind. Continue reading...

articles.summary: Deal deepens company’s relationship with Fifa Dazn paid $1bn for global rights for the 2025 tournament Dazn has secured an exclusive option for global streaming rights for the next men’s Club World Cup in 2029 in a development that deepens its partnership…
articles.content: Deal deepens company’s relationship with Fifa Dazn paid $1bn for global rights for the 2025 tournament Dazn has secured an exclusive option for global streaming rights for the next men’s Club World Cup in 2029 in a development that deepens its partnership with Fifa. The Saudi Arabia-backed ­streaming company came to Fifa’s aid before the inaugural 32-team Club World Cup in the US last year by agreeing to pay $1bn (£745m) for global rights for the tournament after many ­linear broadcasters and other streamers had declined to bid . articles.title: Snowball fight: Cadbury owner in trademark row over festive chocolate treat
articles.summary: Mini Snow Balls’ maker Mondelēz is demanding vegan brand Moo Free remove its White Choccy Snowballs from shelves Toblerone owner sues British vegan chocolate brand over chunky shape The owner of Cadbury and Toblerone has demanded that a small vegan chocolate…
articles.content: Mini Snow Balls’ maker Mondelēz is demanding vegan brand Moo Free remove its White Choccy Snowballs from shelves Toblerone owner sues British vegan chocolate brand over chunky shape The owner of Cadbury and Toblerone has demanded that a small vegan chocolate brand remove its products from shelves in a trademark dispute over the use of the word snowball. Mondelēz International has written a legal letter to Moo Free accusing it of trademark infringement by selling its White Choccy Snowballs – gluten-free biscuit-flavoured rice balls covered in dairy-free white chocolate. articles.title: Sales slump at UK’s largest brickmaker as housebuilding downturn deepens
articles.summary: Ibstock, which has cut production by a fifth, criticises government for delay in help for housing sector Sales at the UK’s largest brickmaker plunged by more than a fifth over the summer, as it criticised the government for not introducing fresh help for the…
articles.content: Ibstock, which has cut production by a fifth, criticises government for delay in help for housing sector Sales at the UK’s largest brickmaker plunged by more than a fifth over the summer, as it criticised the government for not introducing fresh help for the housing sector faster. Leicestershire-based Ibstock said on Monday that sales slumped by 22% below its expectations in the three months to the end of September, prompting it to slash production levels by a fifth.
